results.title: Opera Game, after 9… b5
results.question: Explain the idea behind Stockfish's best move in this position.
results.answer:
Stockfish's top move is 10. Nxb5!, the same move Morphy played here in the Opera Game.

Why it works: 9… b5 attacks the c4 bishop. A routine retreat lets Black catch up in development. Instead, White sacrifices the knight to rip open lines while Black's king is still in the centre and only the queen and one knight are developed. If Black takes with …cxb5, the c4 bishop recaptures on b5 with check. Black's king is stuck, the f6 knight is pinned by Bg5, and White's queen and rooks can join quickly.

Black's best defence is to give back material by trading queens:
10. Nxb5 Qb4+ 11. Qxb4 Bxb4+ 12. c3 cxb5
White then wins the b5 pawn with check and is still clearly winning, about four and a half pawns better [+4.68]. Compare the simpler 10. Bxf6, which is good but only about a pawn and a half better [+1.60].

Lesson: when your opponent is far behind in development, open lines rather than retreating.

To study: replay the Opera Game from the built-in collection. Then read the open games chapter of *Fundamental Chess Openings*.

results.title: 1. e4 e5 2. Qh5 Nc6 3. Bc4: Black to move
results.question: Is there a tactic in the air for either side right now? What should I watch for?
results.answer:
Yes. White is threatening mate right now. The queen on h5 and the bishop on c4 both hit f7, and only your king defends it. If you ignore it, Qxf7 is checkmate (unchecked, not in the engine lines, but easy to verify on the board). This is the classic Scholar's Mate setup. Any "normal" developing move that doesn't cover f7, like ...Nf6, loses on the spot.

Your good options all deal with f7:
- 3…g6 is best, about a third of a pawn better for Black [−0.33]. It blocks the diagonal *and* attacks the loose queen, so you gain time. The engine's main line continues 4. Qd1 Nf6 5. Nc3 Bg7.
- 3…Qe7 defends f7 directly and is also slightly better for Black [−0.16].
- 3…Qf6 holds f7 too but is roughly equal [+0.14]. It blocks your knight's best square.

What to watch next: the early queen is a target. Keep developing with tempo, and note the engine's ...Nd4 idea (move 6 in line 1), which eyes c2.

For the ideas behind this opening, see the chapter on this opening family in *Fundamental Chess Openings*. The Opera Game shows punishing slow development.

results.title: 1. e4 e5 2. Nf3 Nc6 3. Bc4 Nd4 4. Nxe5: Black to move
results.question: Is there a tactic in the air for either side right now? What should I watch for?
results.answer:
Yes, and it's Black's. The key move is 4…Qg5!, a double attack. The queen hits the undefended knight on e5 and the g2 pawn, which shields the rook on h1 and the kingside. White can't easily cover both.

The engine's main line is 4…Qg5 5. Bxf7+ Kd8 6. O-O Qxe5 7. d3 Qf6 8. Bc4. Black wins the knight back for the f-pawn and stands about half a pawn better [−0.57].

What to watch for:
- White's counter-tactics on f7. Both Bxf7+ and Nxf7 (forking queen and h8 rook) are always in the air. That's why quieter replies fail: 4…d5 [+0.77] and 4…Qe7 5. Nxf7 [+0.94] both leave White better.
- Greed punished. If White grabs with 5. Nxf7 (unchecked), the queen and d4 knight can hunt the white king. That's the famous trap behind this gambit.
- Loose pieces. Both h-rooks, the e5 knight and the d4 knight are undefended, so check every capture for a fork.

Note that 4. Nxe5 was the mistake. 4. Nxd4 kept White clearly better [+1.13].

For the ideas, see the chapter on this opening family in *Fundamental Chess Openings* (van der Sterren).

results.title: Queen's Gambit: the Elephant Trap after 6. Nxd5
results.question: Is there a tactic in the air for either side right now? What should I watch for?
results.answer:
Yes. Black wins a piece with 6…Nxd5! This is the famous Elephant Trap, and the engine rates it as winning for Black (about five pawns better for Black [−4.84]).

Why it works:
- White's knight on d5 is attacked and undefended, so 6…Nxd5 simply takes it.
- The "pin" on the f6 knight was an illusion. After 6…Nxd5 7. Bxd8 Bb4+ 8. Qd2 Bxd2+ 9. Kxd2, Black then recaptures on d8. Black gave up the queen but won back White's queen and bishop, finishing a whole knight ahead.
- The key is the check on b4. White can't recapture on d5 because the check comes first.

What to watch for:
- As Black: when your d7 knight blocks the d-file and White grabs on d5, look for Nxd5 followed by Bb4+.
- As White: before taking a "free" pawn, ask whether the pinned piece can move with tempo. Here 6. e3 was correct, keeping a normal, slightly better game for White [+0.37].

For the ideas behind this line, see *Fundamental Chess Openings* by van der Sterren, in the chapter on this opening family.

results.title: A back-rank mate in one
results.question: Explain the idea behind Stockfish's best move in this position.
results.answer:
1. Ra8# is checkmate. It's the classic back-rank mate.

The rook slides from a1 to a8 and checks the king along the 8th rank. Black has no way out:

- No escape squares: f8 and h8 are covered by the rook on the same rank, and f7, g7 and h7 are blocked by Black's own pawns.

- No block or capture: Black has only pawns, and none can reach the 8th rank or take the rook.

So the pawns that normally shelter the king become its prison.

How to spot it: Whenever the enemy king is on its back rank behind unmoved pawns and nothing guards that rank, check whether a rook or queen can reach it. The open a-file gives your rook a direct path to a8.

Lesson for your own games: Give your king *luft* (an escape square) with a timely h3 or g3 when back-rank checks are possible. White has the same weakness here. If Black had a rook, the roles could be reversed.

For more on this pattern, see the Opera Game (Morphy, 1858) in the built-in collection, which also finishes with a back-rank mate.

results.title: Steinitz–von Bardeleben, before 17. d5
results.question: What is the main plan for the side to move here, and why?
results.answer:
The plan is to break open the centre with the isolated pawn while Black's king is stuck on e8. Stockfish's top move is 17. d5!, which leaves White close to two pawns better [+1.75].

Why it works:
- The king is stranded. Black's king can't castle easily, and the knight on e7 is pinned to it by your queen and rook on the e-file. Opening lines now punishes this before Black untangles with ...Kf7 and ...Rhe8.
- 16…c6 helped you. It gave the d-pawn a target, so d5 forces open the c-file for your rook on c1.
- Loose pieces. Both Black rooks are undefended, so open lines and checks create tactics quickly.

A sample engine line: 17. d5 Kf7 18. dxc6 bxc6 19. Qc4+ Qd5. Black's queenside pawns are shattered and his king is still exposed. Slower moves like 17. Qc4 [+0.51] give Black time to consolidate.

General lesson: with an isolated queen's pawn, push it when the opponent's king or pieces are badly placed. Don't let it become a weakness.

Further study:
- Steinitz vs von Bardeleben, Hastings 1895, in the built-in collection. It reached this exact position.
- The Isolated Queen Pawn chapter of *Chess Structures* by Flores Rios.

results.title: King and pawn: Black has the opposition
results.question: What is the main plan for the side to move here, and why?
results.answer:
White's plan is to walk the king in front of the pawn and win the "key squares" d4, e4 and f4, two ranks ahead of the e2-pawn. If White's king reaches one of them, the pawn queens no matter where Black's king is.

The problem is that Black has the opposition: the kings face each other with one square between, and White must move. Whatever White tries, Black mirrors it:

- 1. Kd3 Kd5 or 1. Kf3 Kf5 blocks every outflanking attempt.

- After 1. Kf3 Kf5 2. e4+ Ke5 3. Ke3, Black simply drops back with 3...Kf6. The rule for the defender is to stay in front of the pawn and retake the opposition as it advances.

So the position is a dead draw with correct play (0.00). White should still play it out. Keep the king leading, the pawn behind it, and probe both sides. If Black ever moves off the file in front of the pawn, or loses the opposition, White's king reaches a key square and wins.

For study, try the king and pawn chapters of de la Villa's *100 Endgames You Must Know* (opposition, key squares) or Silman's *Complete Endgame Course*.

results.title: The Lucena position
results.question: Explain the idea behind Stockfish's best move in this position.
results.answer:
1. Rb1 is winning for White (about four and a half pawns better, +4.61). The other two engine moves, 1. Rd1+ and 1. Rc7+, score the same, so the idea matters more than the exact move.

The problem: White's king on b8 blocks its own pawn. It needs to step aside, but Black's king on d7 covers c7 and c8, and the black rook covers the a-file.

The solution: 1. Rb1 puts the rook behind the pawn, guarding it along the b-file. That frees the rook's next job, driving Black's king away with checks:

- Rb1 Ra3 2. Rd1+ Kc6 3. Kc8

Now c8 is free, the king steps out, and b8=Q is threatened. Black's only answer is 3...Rb3 4. b8=Q Rxb8+, giving up the rook for the pawn. White recaptures with the king and has rook against lone king, which is a routine win.

The takeaway: when your king is boxed in front of its pawn, first push the enemy king away with checks, then walk out. This is the core of the Lucena position. Study it in the Lucena and Philidor section of *100 Endgames You Must Know* (de la Villa) and in the built-in Lucena 1497 study.

results.title: The Philidor position: Black to move
results.question: What is the main plan for the side to move here, and why?
results.answer:
Black's plan is the Philidor defence, and the position is a dead draw (about equal, [+0.01]).

Black already has the two things that matter most:

- The king sits on the queening square (e8). It's in front of the pawn, so White can't build a Lucena "bridge" without first driving it away, and there's no way to do that.

- The rook guards the 6th rank. Black's "third-rank defence" (the 6th rank from Black's side) keeps White's king off d6, e6 and f6. While the pawn stays on e5, the king can't advance without walking into checks.

The rule: hold the 6th rank until the pawn advances. Once it reaches e6, the king loses that square as shelter. Then swing the rook down the board and check from behind.

Stockfish shows that Black needn't be rigid. 1… Ra2 2. Rb7 Ra6 is a pure waiting move that returns to the 6th. If White's king does slip forward, distant checks hold: 1… Ra1 2. Ke6 Ra6+ 3. Kf5 Rb6.

Avoid a passive rook on the back rank. That's what loses these endings.

For study, read the Philidor material in de la Villa's *100 Endgames You Must Know* and replay the Philidor 1777 study.

results.title: Sicilian after 3. d4
results.question: What is the main plan for the side to move here, and why?
results.answer:
Black's main plan is to trade the c-pawn for White's d-pawn with 3…cxd4, then develop with tempo against e4. Stockfish rates this best, with White only slightly better (+0.28), which is normal for the opening.

- Why trade? After 3…cxd4 4. Nxd4, Black has two central pawns (d6 and e7) against White's one (e4). That extra centre pawn is a long-term asset. Black also gets the half-open c-file for later rook and queen pressure.

- Follow-up: 4…Nf6 attacks e4 and forces White to spend a move on defence, typically 5. Nc3. Then 5…a6 is the Najdorf: it controls b5 and prepares ...e5 or ...e6 and queenside expansion. The engine continues 6. Bg5.

- Alternatives: 3…Nf6 is almost equal (+0.29) but leads to sharp play after 4. dxc5 Nxe4 5. cxd6 Nc6. 3…Nd7 is passive (+0.71). After 4. dxc5 Nxc5 5. Nc3 a6 6. e5, White gains space and keeps the extra centre pawn.

For the pawn-structure ideas, see the chapter on this opening family in *Fundamental Chess Openings* and Soltis's *Pawn Structure Chess*.
